name: CJC-1295

lead: CJC-1295 is a synthetic analogue of growth hormone releasing hormone. Users take it to raise growth hormone and IGF-1 for recovery, fat loss, skin and sleep, and some younger users hope it adds height.

It binds the GHRH receptor on the pituitary, increasing growth hormone secretion, and the long-acting version attaches to albumin so one dose lifts GH and IGF-1 for days. Early human studies in healthy adults showed prolonged GH and IGF-1 rises. No published trial has shown muscle, fat-loss or cosmetic changes in healthy people.

paras: Used as an injectable research peptide, often combined with the ghrelin mimic ipamorelin, and reported by forum users as prescribed by some clinics. Users usually describe sleep and recovery changes first, with body-composition goals over months.

Not an approved medicine, sold as a research peptide, and banned in sport. A phase II trial was halted after a participant died, though the physician thought it was likely unrelated to the drug. Reported effects include flushing, headache, water retention and injection-site reactions. Long-term safety is unknown and the status of compounded versions has been in flux.

angle.text: CJC-1295 is an injectable peptide taken to raise growth hormone and IGF-1, aiming at better recovery and sleep and a leaner, younger-looking physique. Human data come from a few endocrine studies showing raised GH and IGF-1. The appearance claims rest on user reports.

lead: CJC-1295 is a synthetic analogue of growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH, also called growth hormone-releasing factor) developed by ConjuChem Biotechnologies. It is used in physique and anti-ageing circles as a way to raise growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1) without injecting GH itself, and people who use it describe the hoped-for payoff in appearance terms: a leaner, more muscular physique, fuller recovery between training sessions, better sleep, firmer-looking skin and, in some looksmaxxing threads, extra height or bone mass.[1][2][3] The chain proponents describe runs from a GH and IGF-1 rise to better recovery and body composition, and from there to a better-looking physique.

In its best-known form, CJC-1295 with a 'drug affinity complex' (DAC), the peptide attaches to the blood protein albumin, which gives it a half-life of roughly six to eight days in humans and lets a single injection raise GH and IGF-1 for days.[1][4][5] A shorter-acting version without the DAC, usually called 'modified GRF (1-29)' or 'CJC-1295 no DAC', is a separate compound, although the two names are often confused and Wikipedia notes that several scientific papers have equated them.[1] Forum users frequently pair either version with ipamorelin, a ghrelin-receptor agonist that also triggers GH release.[3][6][7]

Published human work on CJC-1295 consists of early-phase trials in healthy adults, which showed prolonged GH and IGF-1 stimulation, and a phase II trial in people with HIV and visceral obesity that was terminated after a participant died; the attending physician thought the death most likely reflected undiagnosed coronary artery disease unrelated to the drug.[4][5][1][8] No published trial has measured muscle, fat loss, height or cosmetic outcomes in healthy people.[9][10]

CJC-1295 is not an approved medicine anywhere. It is sold as a research peptide, some forum users report receiving it from clinics, and it is prohibited in sport by the World Anti-Doping Agency.[1][6][10] Recent reviews of peptide use in sport and aesthetics describe the human evidence as limited and point to the risks of mislabelled or contaminated products from an unregulated supply chain.[11][10]
infobox: CJC-1295 DAC, DAC:GRF; 'modified GRF (1-29)' is the version without DAC[1]
Single dose: GH raised 2- to 10-fold for 6 days or more; IGF-1 raised 1.5- to 3-fold for 9 to 11 days[4]
Listed as nominated but withdrawn; FDA cites immunogenicity and limited clinical data[26]

paras: Outside trials, CJC-1295 is used by bodybuilders, gym-goers and people interested in anti-ageing to increase GH and IGF-1 secretion. A 2016 netnographic study of internet forums found female users who chose it for weight loss, muscle enhancement, youthful skin, better sleep and injury healing.[2] Users on T Nation describe it in nightly or weekly injection 'stacks' with ipamorelin or GHRP-6, and a looksmax.org thread on the combination lists benefits users expect, including collagen synthesis, recovery, sleep quality and anti-ageing.[12][6][3]

In looksmaxxing communities the discussion has an extra strand: height and facial or skeletal growth. Teenagers whose growth plates are still open ask on looksmax.org whether the pairing can add height or bone mass, and other members reply with scepticism or point to human GH as the alternative.[3][13][14] No published study has tested CJC-1295 for height or bone structure.

CJC-1295 has no approved medical use. It was developed as a longer-lasting alternative to the older GHRH fragment sermorelin and was studied for growth hormone deficiency and for HIV-associated lipodystrophy and visceral obesity before development stopped.[1][8] Sermorelin itself was approved by the US FDA in 1997, mainly as a diagnostic agent, and its manufacturer discontinued it in 2008 for commercial rather than safety reasons.[15]

CJC-1295 is a modified form of the first 29 amino acids of GHRH (the sequence also known as sermorelin) with four amino acid substitutions that make it resistant to enzymatic breakdown. The DAC version carries a maleimidopropionyl group on a lysine at position 30, which bonds covalently to albumin after injection.[1][16][17] Wikipedia notes that CJC-1295, CJC-1295 DAC and CJC-1295 with DAC are synonyms, whereas 'modified GRF (1-29)' lacks that group and has been wrongly equated with it in some papers.[1]

The distinction matters in practice because the two products behave differently: the albumin-bound form persists for days, while the unconjugated analogue is cleared quickly. Forum threads comparing 'with DAC' and 'no DAC' are common on looksmax.org.[1][18]

CJC-1295 binds the GHRH receptor on pituitary somatotroph cells and increases GH secretion; in rats, the albumin-bound analogue was shown to be long-lasting.[17] Because it works upstream, through the pituitary, it acts within the body's own feedback loop rather than replacing GH. Ipamorelin, the usual partner, acts on a different receptor: it is a selective agonist of the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor with an elimination half-life of about two hours, originally developed by Novo Nordisk and later tested by Helsinn in a phase II trial for postoperative ileus that was discontinued.[7]

In two randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind ascending-dose trials of 28 and 49 days in healthy adults aged 21 to 61, a single injection produced dose-dependent rises in mean GH of 2- to 10-fold lasting six days or more, and in mean IGF-1 of 1.5- to 3-fold lasting 9 to 11 days; with repeated doses IGF-1 stayed above baseline for up to 28 days, and the estimated half-life was 5.8 to 8.1 days.[4]

A companion study in healthy men aged 20 to 40 sampled blood every 20 minutes overnight before and a week after one injection. Pulsatile GH secretion was preserved, with pulse frequency and size unchanged, while trough GH rose about 7.5-fold, mean GH rose 46% and IGF-1 rose 45%.[5] A later analysis of the same program reported changes in serum protein profiles consistent with activation of the GH/IGF-1 axis.[19]

ConjuChem developed CJC-1295 in the mid-2000s as part of a program to extend the life of peptide drugs by attaching them to albumin. In 2005, researchers led by Jetté reported that GRF(1-29)-albumin bioconjugates activated the GRF receptor in rats and identified CJC-1295 as a long-lasting analogue.[17][1] A phase II trial in HIV-infected patients with visceral obesity (NCT00267527) was registered with a start of December 2005 and enrolment listed at 120, and it is recorded as terminated.[8]

In 2006 the first human trial reports appeared in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism, alongside an animal paper on once-daily dosing in GHRH-deficient mice.[4][5][20][1] A ConjuChem report from August 2006 described the death of a participant in the clinical program; the attending physician attributed it most likely to asymptomatic coronary artery disease with plaque rupture and considered it unrelated to CJC-1295, but development was ended as a precaution.[1]

The peptide then moved into the grey market. In 2009 Norwegian police and customs submitted an unknown preparation that analysts identified as CJC-1295, and a 2014 report described confiscations of the peptide in Denmark between 2007 and 2013.[21][1] Anti-doping laboratories developed methods to detect it, culminating in reviews of detection for GHRH analogues in 2021.[22][23][24]

The human literature on CJC-1295 is concentrated in 2006 and 2009. The two ascending-dose trials in healthy adults examined pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and safety and reported prolonged GH and IGF-1 stimulation, with the authors describing no serious adverse reactions and relatively good tolerability at the doses tested.[4] The pulsatility study showed that continuous stimulation did not abolish GH pulses.[5] The serum protein study described effects on the GH/IGF-1 axis in normal adults.[19] Once-daily administration was examined in a GHRH-knockout mouse model, where it normalised growth in the animals.[20][1]
The phase II trial in HIV patients with visceral obesity was terminated and no efficacy results from it have been published in the literature reviewed here.[8][1]

No trial has assessed CJC-1295 for muscle growth, athletic performance, body composition, skin or other cosmetic outcomes in healthy adults. A 2026 narrative review of injectable peptide therapy for orthopaedic and sports medicine physicians and a 2026 review of peptide use in sport describe the human evidence for GHRH analogues and ipamorelin as limited, and a review of aesthetic and endocrine peptides concludes that further studies are needed before most newer peptides can be used safely in humans.[9][10][25]

The long-term safety of CJC-1295 is unknown. Reviews of peptide use in sport warn of cardiovascular strain, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia and psychiatric instability associated with GH-axis agents used outside trial conditions, and note that products from an unregulated supply chain are often mislabelled or contaminated.[10] A review of approved and unapproved peptides in sports medicine says rigorous human safety data for unapproved peptides are scarce and that potential for serious harm exists.[11]

The US FDA, in describing why it has restricted certain peptides in compounding, states that CJC-1295 may carry immunogenicity risk because of peptide-related impurities and the complexity of characterising the substance, and that it has been associated with serious adverse events including increased heart rate and a systemic vasodilatory reaction, with limited clinical data available.[26] The same page lists ipamorelin acetate in its category 2 table, added on 29 September 2023.[26]

Users report side effects of their own. One T Nation poster describes pronounced hunger and a 'hypo' feeling when combining CJC-1295 with GHRP-6.[12] The female-user netnography recorded concerns about estimating dose, cycling and long-term consequences given sex differences in GH pulses.[2] The looksmax.org thread on bone mass and height lists immunogenicity, increased heart rate, flushing, warmth and transient hypotension among the possible negatives.[3]

subs.h: Use in physique and looksmaxxing communities
paras: On T Nation, posters describe running CJC-1295 with ipamorelin or GHRP-6. One reports choosing it after a distal biceps tendon surgery and returning to full duty ahead of schedule, another describes a clinic prescribing the CJC-1295 and ipamorelin pair, another credits a CJC/ipamorelin/GHRP-2 blend plus kisspeptin for a return of libido, and a poster who says he is 67 describes nightly injections that raised a very low IGF-1.[27][6][28][29] Posters in older threads from around 2008 to 2011 discuss GHRP-6 and modified GRF (1-29) as a cheaper alternative to GH.[12][30][31]

On looksmax.org the compound shows up in threads about height, bone mass, facial growth and skin. One thread frames the combination as a 'safer' alternative to GH, while a reply argues it costs as much as GH and offers no reason to choose it; other replies dismiss it as unlikely to add much height.[3][14] Several threads are started by teenagers asking about its use before growth plates close.[13] Posts of this kind often cite dosing websites and vendor information that the wiki does not reproduce.

GHRH analogues are prohibited by WADA, and analytical papers describe immunoaffinity purification and mass-spectrometry methods developed to detect CJC-1295 and related peptides in blood and urine.[24][22][23][10] The compound has no approved status in any major market, and Wikipedia classes it as an abandoned drug.[1]

In the United States, compounding pharmacies may only use bulk substances that meet FDA criteria. The agency's public table lists CJC-1295 among substances that were nominated and then withdrawn, and notes the safety concerns above.[26]

Sermorelin is the unmodified GHRH(1-29) fragment from which CJC-1295 is derived; it was FDA-approved in 1997 and discontinued in 2008, and may still be obtained through compounding.[15] Ipamorelin, GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 are the ghrelin-receptor agonists usually stacked with GHRH analogues. Recombinant human GH is the reference alternative that users compare cost and safety against. Other peptides, such as BPC-157 and TB-500, are discussed alongside it in injury-recovery threads.[27][12]

lore.intro: On T Nation and looksmax.org, CJC-1295 is discussed as the GHRH half of a 'CJC plus ipamorelin' pairing meant to raise GH and IGF-1 without injecting GH, for physique, recovery, skin, sleep and sometimes height.[3][6][2][12]
